utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As the court closed yesterday afternoon, the accused made a request to the legal officers for a copy of the joint statement of November the 1st of 1995 reflecting the point at the evidence where we reached yesterday. That's been provided to him but I'm not going to ask the witness any questions myself arising from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ambassador Galbraith, after the meeting you described yesterday ended, did you indeed return to press on with negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you return to Dayton or was your time at Dayton limited?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to Dayton at the very end, but that is to say after the peace agreement in Croatia had been signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The conversation that you had with the accused and that you told us about yesterday, was that reflected in or confirmed by or countered by conversations you had with Milan Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we resumed the negotiations which involved a shuttle between Zagreb or sometimes Osijek and Erdut in Eastern Slavonia, we were not making any progress, and at one point Milan Milanovic told me -- we had presented a new and revised draft, and at one point, I thinks it was November 5th, November 5th or 6th he said, "Well, I'll sign this draft if Milosevic tells me to do so."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your understanding, what level of influence or control did the accused have over the Eastern Slavonia part of the Dayton negotiations until the conclusion of those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was completely clear to me that we were not going to have an agreement until the accused decided that there would be an agreement, and that would depend not on any circumstance in Eastern Slavonia but it would depend on when he found it convenient in the Dayton process, that is, in the overall process, to reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to that overall process, you can, of course, speak of what you saw yourself, of what you were told by others, but Eastern Slavonia apart, the rest of it was dealt with by others?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dealt in a very limited way with some of the Bosnia issues and Federation, but it was a very small role.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 471, I think it is, tab 2. If that could just be made available. Tell us about this agreement without taking us through the detail of it.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Erdut agreement of the 12th of November, 1995. This is the Croatia peace agreement that provided for the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem into Croatia after a one or two-year transitional period. You will notice that this is a 14-point agreement, and it is substantially the same as what was agreed to on October 3rd, also in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That leaves one general topic, then. You've spoken of the accused's resistance to offers and plans in respect of Eastern Slavonia. You've explained to us something about the majority of Serbs requirement or the requirement that there be a majority of Serbs for autonomy under the Z-4 plan. What was the reason revealed to you from your negotiations for the accused's reluctance to conclude an agreement for Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, to put -- there was a larger context here. It's my judgement that at the beginning of the Croatia war and indeed perhaps at the beginning of the Bosnia war, it was the hope of the accused to be able to create a Greater Serbia carved out of most of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as the -- a sizeable part of Croatia. Obviously the Krajina region, Eastern Slavonia, Western Slavonia, and the Dubrovnik region. By 1993, 1994, that obviously was not attainable, but I think it was his hope that he could make a deal in which he would trade -- he would allow Croatia to recover the Krajina, probably militarily in exchange for which there would be some kind of territorial settlement in which Serbia would acquire some Croatian territory in Eastern Slavonia, either the entire region, which was very rich farmland and which included oil, or a part of it. And in this he was encouraged, if my view, by one of the international mediators, Lord David Owen who did speak frequently about the possibility of territorial exchanges, although the international community, both the United States and the European Union, completely opposed any border changes, especially those that came about by force. Nonetheless, he engaged in those discussions. I must also say that from time to time, President Tudjman indicated or perhaps sent signals that he may have been interested in giving up at least part of Eastern Slavonia. So I think that too may have encouraged the defendant to believe that such an arrangement was possible. I also think that he -- I don't think that he had any interest in the welfare of the Serbs that lived in the Krajina, and I think he looked at the Z-4 plan as not for what it might have done for the Serbs of Krajina which is to have allowed them to remain in Croatia and to have had substantial autonomy but, rather, as a precedent that might be applied to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, before you move on, just to qualify that and it's the last thing I want to deal with I suspect, can you give us your source for this proposition, namely his linking it to and forecasting difficulties with Kosovo if autonomy was granted in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from international mediators who dealt with him, and also this was something that Hrvoje Sarinic, Tudjman's Chief of Staff who had a number of meetings with him also said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just to crystallise it, his concern was what as you understood it from those sources?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: His concern was that if the Krajina had a high degree of autonomy such as was envisioned in the Z-4 plan, the Krajina being a minority community within Croatia, a local majority but a minority within the entire country, it would create a precedent for the Albanian majority in Kosovo to have the same kind of autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ambassador. You will be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're not getting any interpretation. Can you start again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpreters now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croatian World Congress on the 4th of July 2002 submitted a formal application to Mrs. Del Ponte to start an investigation against retired US army officers for assistance they gave to Operations Flash and Storm and also against a few officials of the United States of America, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that that has taken place, or at least I've seen reports of it on the Internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance, Mr. May, is that in this Operation Storm that Mr. Galbraith has been testifying about, the greatest crime was committed against the Serbs. Over 250.000 persons were expelled from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't make a speech. Just try and make the point shortly. Now, what is the point you're trying to put to the witness, instead of making a speech about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is that a crime was committed against the Serbs in Croatia in this operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're not going to get anywhere like this. What is the point that you want the witness to deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I got my answer, that he did know about it, that the World Croatian Congress committed a formal request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know what "relevance" means. What is the relevance of it even if it's right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance, Mr. May, is that Mr. Galbraith, no doubt throughout his testimony, has been justifying this crime and explaining it with some political reasoning that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. We now have the relevance and it can be put to the witness. What is suggested, Ambassador, is that your evidence is, I suppose, biased, it's being said, and that you were concerned to justify your role and the role, no doubt, of the United States. How would you respond to that allegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the United States did everything possible to try to bring about a peaceful solution to the Krajina problem. We devoted enormous effort at considerable expense to our relations with Croatia to come up with a plan, a viable plan that would have provided very substantial autonomy. We pursued this even up until the very last minute. I explained yesterday the very difficult circumstances, the very difficult choices that we were presented with in July of 1995 when we were faced with the dilemma of having to choose between the possible -- likely fall of Bihac and the probable massacre of 40.000 men and boys, assuming that the Bosnian Serbs did exactly the same thing there that they had done a week before, ten days before, in Srebrenica, and what would be the consequences of Croatian military action, which we anticipated likely would create a lot of refugees. It was a terrible dilemma and we tried everything we could to avoid that, to find a peaceful settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you've raised the question of Bihac, Mr. Galbraith, do you know that this was not a conflict at all between the forces of Republika Srpska or the forces of the Republika Srpska Krajina with the 5th Corps that was in Bihac? It was a Muslim/Muslim conflict, because the entire area had been proclaimed the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia, and its president was Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue that took place in July of 1995 was not about the Muslim/Muslim conflict, the conflict between Abdic and the 5th Corps. It was an attack by the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina across an international border into an United Nations safe area of Bihac and a simultaneous attack by the Bosnian Serb army into Bihac in circumstances where we had every reason to expect that there would be systematic killing of thousands of people if the attackers prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here the declaration. The opposing side has it, and I received an English translation from them. The 23rd of October is the date. Radovan Karadzic and Fikret Abdic concluded a peace agreement thereby and made it possible to fully normalise relations between them and the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia. In it it says: "Motivated" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness should have a copy of this. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll try and find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give the witness this declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- once I've pointed out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll try and find a copy of it. In the meanwhile, carry on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an English translation, so Mr. Galbraith can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says: [In English] "Securing a durable peace between the Serbs and Muslims in the area of former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the president of the Republika Srpska Radovan Karadzic and the president of Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, the Republic of Bosnia, Fikret Abdic, have met in Belgrade and decided to propose jointly and with the involvement of president of Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, the following declaration." [Interpretation] And then this declaration which has about 12 paragraphs, and it was signed on the 22nd of October, 1993. And this indicates a full normalisation of their relations, mutual respect, freedom of movement, economic, political and every other form of cooperation, and it was signed by the president of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, the president of the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia, of the Republic of Bosnia, Fikret Abdic. I did too, but it says, "Witness to the agreement achieved [In English] and assuming the obligation to mediate in the case of difficulties arising in its implementation, [Interpretation] president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic." You can have a look at the declaration. So the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia was recognised, and everybody thought that this was a major step towards peace, because at least over there, all hostilities had ceased between the Serbs and Muslims. However, there were hostilities between Muslims and Alija Izetbegovic's 5th Corps which was stationed in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Ambassador, have you got a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any comment would you like to make about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see what the point is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the moment, that's the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an attack from the Republika Srpska Krajina and the Bosnian Serb army on Bihac, and it was -- the Bihac enclave was in danger of falling. That remains the situation that existed in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And is it right that it refers to the possibility of mediation by the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I haven't had the chance to -- I mean, I haven't had the chance to look through this document. I'll do so. Well, in fact, and I have to say I've skimmed it because I know the defendant doesn't have a lot of time, I actually don't see a reference here to the defendant being -- having a role of mediating. What I do see is that Karadzic and Abdic expressed their gratitude for the great contribution he has given to the arrangement of just and durable peace between the Republika Srpska and the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia of the Republic of Bosnia. But just to set the record straight, the problem here is that Abdic was not in control of Bihac. It is true that Abdic was aligned with the Serbian side, but he was not in control of Bihac, and so I don't quite understand the relevance of all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Galbraith, in view of the fact that you were then ambassador to Croatia, that Mr. Abdic, just as he came to see me, visited President Tudjman even more often? And he also established good relations with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly know that he was a regular visitor to Croatia, and indeed he took up residence in Rijeka. He was given or has Croatian citizenship. He met with Hrvoje Sarinic, and indeed on at least one occasion I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he did meet with Tudjman too, as you know; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I have no reason to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia could not have constituted a danger for Croatia, and the forces of Fikret Abdic wanted to have the entire territory under their control, and they wanted to expel Alija Izetbegovic's 5th Corps from there altogether. Is that right or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure Fikret Abdic did wish to defeat the 5th Corps and establish his control over all of Bihac, but he didn't. Bihac was mostly controlled by Dudakovic and the 5th Corps, and they were being attacked by the RSK forces and by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You believe that they were not being attacked by Fikret Abdic's forces?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Fikret Abdic was at various times a minor ally of the RSK. Again, the attack that came across the international border was an attack by forces of the army of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the position taken by Belgrade, that no one should interfere in this conflict, regardless of the fact that there was an alliance and that the leaderships of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina had a very good understanding with Fikret Abdic and his leadership and that they cooperated as well?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine that if you wish to launch an attack, you might be able to find somebody from the other side. In other words, if you're the Serbian side and you want to attack the Bihac enclave, you might be able to find some Muslim from the Bihac enclave who could be on your side. That doesn't change the fact that this was an attack by the Bosnian Serb army and the Republika Srpska Krajina army, and it wasn't an attack by the Abdic forces. They may have been involved, but it was fundamentally an attack by the two Serbian armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the fact that Abdic held the majority of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia, which was recognised by the Republika Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska as well as the Republic of Croatia, which also had problems -- which also had good relations with Abdic, isn't that proof that the AP of Western Bosnia, including Bihac, could not jeopardise Croatia at all? As you said yourself, Abdic even had Croatian citizenship. He lived in Rijeka in addition to Kladusa in the AP of Western Bosnia. So wasn't that a pretext to attack Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abdic controlled a part of the Bihac enclave part of the time. Most of the Bihac enclave was controlled by the 5th Corps, and that certainly was true of Bihac town. Croatia's concern was that if the Bihac enclave collapsed, if it was overrun by the Bosnian Serb army and the RSK, that then there could be created a single western Serb state. The unification of the RSK and the Republika Srpska, and there would be no internal lines, that is the Serb forces would not be facing forces in Bihac. They could transfer their forces to the Krajina front and it would become impossible for Croatia to recover its territory. That was their strategic concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know very well what the official position taken by Belgrade was, that Belgrade in fact did not agree with any kind of unification of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina at all, which was initiated, and it was written about in the press. It was no secret that that was the subject of negotiations between the leadership of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina on several occasions. And Belgrade considered this to be completely untenable. I'm sure you'll remember that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember statements to that effect, but I also know that at the same time, you were supporting the armies of both Serbian entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We supported Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina for them to survive. That is not challenged at all. We did assist them in that respect. And you yourself said that it was a very poor area which would not have been able to survive without assistance from us, without food, without medicines, and all the other types of aid and assistance that we afforded them. What's strange in that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you what's strange. If you were genuinely concerned with the survival of the Serbs in the Krajina, why didn't you come out and support a plan that would have provided them with very substantial autonomy, that would have enabled them to stay there? Why, on the 2nd and 3rd of August, didn't you meet with Babic? Why on the 2nd and 3rd of August -- or the 3rd of August did you refuse to meet with Rudy Perina, the American Charge? Why didn't you send that word that could have stopped the tragedy that overtook the Serbs of the Krajina? That's why I don't understand. Why did you refuse to meet us in January of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll explain why. It's take it in order. I'm the one asking questions, and I'm going to ask you questions. Do you happen to recall, Mr. Galbraith -- let's be fair here in observance of the facts at least, nothing else, nothing more than that -- that on the 19th of January, 1994, that is to say a year and a half before all these events came to pass, in the Geneva Palace of Nations a joint declaration was signed on the gradual normalisation of relations between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Croatia, and that provided for the opening up of official representative offices on the part of the two governments in Belgrade and Zagreb respectively to facilitate inter-state relations and contacts and to contribute to building up mutual trust and confidence between the two sides, including the process of normalisation for Serbo-Croatian relations. And this is what was set up in that statement, in the declaration signed by the Foreign Ministers of Yugoslavia, by Radoslav Jovanovic and the Foreign Minister of Croatia, Mate Granic, in the presence of the president of Republic of Croatia and Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must have a question. Ambassador -- just a moment -- you're being asked about this agreement on the 19th of January, 1994. Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recollect such an agreement. I obviously don't precisely remember the date, but yes, there was such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, at the time, in the presence of Tudjman, myself, and the others, the two Ministers signed this declaration on normalisation, and we considered that the future of the relationships lay in confidence-building measures, in creating good relation the between Croatia and Yugoslavia, whereas the questions that remain open and unsettled had to be solved by political means, on a Knin-Zagreb relationship. Was that true, Mr. Galbraith? It wasn't up to Yugoslavia itself, but it was the normalisation of relations that was initiated, and the questions would be solved between Knin and Zagreb. Is that right, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were the decisive factor in whether there was going to be a settlement between Zagreb and Knin. You were the one who called the shots, and this was demonstrated in the Eastern Slavonia process where the lead Serb negotiator, Milan Milanovic, basically went to Belgrade before every negotiating session and where the final deal was not concluded in the negotiations that Stoltenberg and I were conducting between Zagreb and Erdut, but it was concluded in Dayton when you and President Tudjman, in the presence of Secretary Christopher, concluded the final agreement using the document that in fact had been worked out on October 3rd. That was when the deal was done. The paper was then brought by Hrvoje Sarinic to Zagreb. I was under very clear instructions that there were to be no changes, and indeed there weren't, and it was signed. And incidentally, unlike Bosnia where at least you had the so-called patriarch document, that is the document signed by Karadzic and Mladic and others saying that you could make decisions on their behalf, there wasn't even a comparable document here. You just went ahead and did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I suppose the question which the accused was asking and which perhaps you would deal with is this: Assuming, and I'll try and get a copy of this to see if it's correct, but assuming for the moment there there was an understanding in Geneva that matters were to be resolved between Knin and Zagreb, was that put into effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, unfortunately, the facts overall what you're saying. You say that in Dayton we signed an agreement. I did not have it, and I asked the Registrar of the Tribunal to provide me a copy of the agreement and I received it this morning when I came into the courtroom here. And because it was considered that it was by this agreement -- let me put it this way: On my part and Croatia's part that the question was solved, the question of Eastern Slavonia. I really would like, as the agreement is a very short one, for us to establish that that is not correct. Here is what it says in the agreement, and we can put it on the overhead projector, perhaps. It says: "Joint statement --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have copies. Let's all have copies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have copies to distribute, then you can read what it says and bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But before we do so, let's clear up one point. We came to Dayton to solve the question of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's right, isn't it, Mr. Galbraith? Peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although it was not going to be possible to get a peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina without also getting a peace agreement that provided for the return of Eastern Slavonia to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, take a look at what you call an agreement. This is a joint declaration, in fact, and this is what it says: "President Tudjman and Milosevic [In English] Requesting Ambassador Galbraith and Mr. Stoltenberg to resume negotiation." [Interpretation] That is the title, the heading, which is like a journalistic one, "Dayton Ohio, the 1st of November, 1995" and then it says under the auspices of Secretary Christopher, President Tudjman and Milosevic met at the carriage house, [In English] Dayton, Wright-Patterson Airbase. They agreed to a peaceful resolution of the Eastern Slavonia question and -- and asked Ambassador Galbraith and Mr. Stoltenberg to resume their mediation efforts." [Interpretation] So the mediation efforts between Knin and Zagreb. And then it goes on to say: "Ambassador Galbraith prepared a statement that the two presidents signed." And what does it say in that statement? Now, this is the actual text of the statement. You refer to it as an agreement and solution and my decision about this solution. Here is what it says: [In English] "At the question of Secretary Christopher, President Tudjman and President Milosevic met this afternoon." [Interpretation] That meeting, as you will remember, was not scheduled, and I wasn't late because I was informed about it later on. [In English] "Agreed to form toward a full normalisation of relations between their countries on the basis of ..." [Interpretation] That means that we are agreeing to work toward full normalisation between our two countries on the following basis. And then there are just three points. Actually, they're not numbered, these points, but it just says paragraphs: "[In English] [Previous translation continues]... human rights for all citizens of their countries." [Interpretation] That's the first point. [In English] "All refugees and displaced persons in the two countries to return to their homes and to recover their property or to receive just compensation." [Interpretation] And the third point: [In English] "Support for a solution to the problem of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, as rapidly as possible on the basis of negotiations between the government of Croatia and the representatives of the Serbian people in the area." [Interpretation] So those are the three points, Mr. Galbraith. No agreement did we manage to reach, but we did precisely what I claimed we did, and that is that between the government in Zagreb and the representatives of the Serb people in the area, a solution should be found through negotiation. And finally it says, in this spirit: [In English] "Ambassador Galbraith and Mr. Stoltenberg to return to the region tomorrow to continue, on an intensified basis, their mediation." [Interpretation] And that's all it says. Therefore, this confirms that the problem must be solved, had to be solved between the representatives of the Croatian government and the Serb representatives for the Serbs in the region. So we didn't in fact reach an agreement of any kind between Tudjman and myself or, rather, I not decide what Eastern Slavonia was going to look like. And here you have that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must come to a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could deal with that, Ambassador, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is not an agreement on Eastern Slavonia, and this is not the agreement to which I was referring. The agreement to which I was referring is the Erdut agreement of the 12th of November. And the final text of that agreement, which is obviously very similar to the one of the 3rd of October, but that final text was worked out between you and President Tudjman in the presence of Secretary Christopher and Chris Hill in Dayton. And specifically, there was one issue that was unresolved from the 3rd of October, which was the length of the transitional period. And it was you who worked it out with President Tudjman that it would be one year, possibly renewable. That text incorporating that point was then hand-carried to me by Hrvoje Sarinic, as well as sent by fax, with instructions that none of it was going to be changed because this is what the two presidents had agreed to. That is the agreement to which I'm referring. And incidentally, if you're maintaining that this was all to be worked out in the region, why in the very meeting were you and President Tudjman agreed to this statement, why in that very meeting did you then raise substantive issues, such as insisting that there should be a referendum?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We'll give a number to the joint statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit number 151, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, a moment ago we took a look at what we signed in Dayton here, that is to say that we wanted to see a normalisation of relations and that we strove for a respect of the internationally recognised human rights, that the refugees should return, all of them, and that we lent our support to a peaceful solution to the problem and that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that depended on the government in Zagreb and the representative of the Serbs in the Eastern Slavonia area, and that's how it was. That's what happened. And that's all we signed, and that is what you gave us as a draft. And then in the negotiations that followed, you, as the mediators, and as far as I was able to see from the papers I consulted, I was able to see that on behalf of the representative of the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, this was signed by Milanovic whom you mentioned a moment ago and on behalf of the international community it was Stoltenberg, and you witnessed it as the witness. Isn't that so, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that it was signed by Milanovic, myself, Stoltenberg, and Hrvoje Sarinic, but that does not mean that the final text was negotiated by us. The final text was negotiated by you in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Galbraith. I don't have time to spare on that issue. We have it as an exhibit, and we see the three points in the document and the agreement signed by you and Milanovic also exists. Not as an agreement between myself and Tudjman but as an agreement between myself and the government of the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you have a question, you can ask it, but you're not making comments here. It's something we may have to determine in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, apart from the fact that I explained how the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia was a threat to Croatia and that that was the basis for Croatia to attack Knin, did you as the US Ambassador to Croatia, were you actually conscious of the fact that it was completely illegal that in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were regular Croatian troops present? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. Milosevic, I never said that the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia was a threat to Croatia, and I don't agree with that. What I said was that the Bosnian Serb -- that the Croatians, that the Croatians felt that the Bosnian Serb -- a Bosnian Serb and RSK army takeover of Bihac would be a serious -- would do serious harm to the interests of Croatia. That's what I said. Now, as to your second question, yes, we were aware that at various times the Croatian army was present in Bosnia, and we did consider that at certain times to be illegal. However, there was a point in time when we considered it to be legal, and that was when the internationally recognised Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina invited the Croatian army to come and provide assistance to it, and that took place in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But let's just clear up one point, Mr. May. Did you take as an exhibit this agreement between Karadzic and Abdic? Has it been exhibited on the peace signing between the Republika Srpska and the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, which actually explains the actual situation as it was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know if we've had that yet. We'll give that the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 152, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, is it true and correct that in fact throughout all those years, apart from the Croatian side, there were no attacks on the part of Republika Srpska Krajina launched against the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, take a look then at the 16th of July, 1993, a document here. The government of the Republic of Croatia and the Republika Srpska Krajina in Erdut signed an agreement according to which Croatia was bound by the 31st of July, and we're talking about 1993, to withdraw its troops from occupied territories of Republika Srpska Krajina, Ravni Kotari and Maslenica, the Miljevac plateau, the hydroelectric power station Peruca, the airport in return for opening the bridge over the Maslenica canal and the canal in Zemunik. So before that they had stormed the area which was under UN protection, and on the 16th of July, 1993, they agreed that the Croatian army should withdraw from the area and in return they would open up the bridge across the Maslenica canal and the approaches to the Zemunik airport. Is that right, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean I -- there was an agreement somewhat along those lines. I would have to look at that specific document that you're citing. I would -- I'm not sure where this is leading, but I mean, I would also have to note that subsequent to that, the Krajina Serb forces launched artillery on the pontoon bridge at Maslenica that the Croatians had built.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness look at the document. If you want to rely on the document, let the witness see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the document here. I have a chronology of events here, and I assume that Mr. Galbraith knows about these events, is familiar with them. Now, if he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Depends where you get the chronology from, but you could certainly put it to the witness and it will be up to him whether he can agree to it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did put it to the witness. Now, if he claims that there was no agreement in Erdut with the following contents, I'll move on with my questions. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you'll remember that, Mr. Galbraith. Do you in fact remember it or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said to you, there was at some point in there an agreement that provided for the opening of the airport by Zadar and the bridge, but in the absence of having the chronology or the documents, I can't say that, you know, what the details of the document were. I mean, there was an agreement along the lines that you suggest at a certain point in time, quite likely as you say on the 16th of July. It's just you're asking me to vouch for something when, you know, I frankly can't remember the specific date and the details of the document. But it sounds right. It sounds like something like that happened around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I accept your answer. Yes, I do. Now, do you remember this -- it will be something closer to you because it was an international document, that the February Resolution 802 of the UN Security Council made it incumbent upon the parties, just like the Erdut agreement, that the Croatian army withdraw from those territories. And I'm talking about a UN Security Council Resolution now. It's number is 802. Because this jeopardised the agreement that had been reached, the basic elements of the Vance Plan that was being put into practice in the region?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sounds right. I do recall a Security Council Resolution. Quite likely it was Resolution 802. Without the resolution I can't say definitively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, it's easy to ascertain all this because there are documents. We can refer to them.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt that. I just don't have these documents before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, Mr. Galbraith, that on the 4th of February, 1994, the Security Council, UN Security Council --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- adopted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness is just being handed a document. I don't know where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Defence Exhibit 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you just tell us what it is, Ambassador, so we know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document I've just been given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's UN Security Council Resolution 802, and it -- let me -- I could read it. It demands the immediate cessation of hostilities by Croatian armed forces within or adjacent to the United Nations Protected Areas and the withdrawal of Croatian armed forces from these areas. It condemns attacks on UNPROFOR personnel. It demands that the heavy weapons ceased from UNPROFOR-controlled storage areas be returned immediately to UNPROFOR. It -- which I think were the Serbian -- taken by the Serbs. It demands that all parties and others concerned comply strictly with the cease-fire arrangements already agreed, cooperate fully and unconditionally in the implementation of the United Nations peacekeeping plan, expresses its condolences to the family of UNPROFOR personnel who have lost their lives, demands that all parties and others concerned respect the safety of United Nations personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've got it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would note this is 25 January, 1993, which was actually was about five months before I took up my duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we're not disputing the fact, I assume, that this was a Croatian attack on the protected areas; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can only say what's in the document. It's before his time. Now, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 4th of February, 1994, the UN Security Council adopted a presidential statement cautioning Croatia that it will be subjected to serious consequences if within the space of two weeks it fails to reduce its regular military units from Bosnia? And the point of my question now is was it clear and well known that ever since 1992, regular Croatian forces were stationed in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm very familiar with that presidential statement of the 4th of February, 1994. It was my job to convey to the -- to President Tudjman and other Croatian officials in the strongest possible terms our insistence that they withdraw their regular military forces, that they stop the attacks on the forces of the Bosnian government, and to warn that there would be serious consequences including the likelihood of sanctions. Incidentally, something I also stated publicly in a speech I gave at the Lisinski concert hall on the 17th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galbraith, let us try and do this in some logical order. You have seen this agreement on a normalisation of relations between Yugoslavia and Croatia. I assume that you will recollect that the position of Serbia and my own personal position was that as far as final solutions were concerned, there were three significant steps that needed to be made, and those were in the following order: First of all, the cessation of all hostilities, followed by a normalisation of economic relations, and thirdly, a political settlement. A cessation of all hostilities, in a sense, is a precondition for the beginning of the normalisation of economic relations, and the normalisation of those relations, as a result of which life will encourage the parties to cooperate and is a precondition for a fair political settlement for existing problems. Was that not, from the very beginning, the position held by Serbia and me personally?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have described the Z-4 process in which we engaged, which indeed began with a cease-fire, was followed by an effort to reach an agreement on economics -- economic and confidence-building measures and meant to be followed by a political settlement. The difficulty was that the Krajina Serbs refused to engage seriously for a very long period of time on the economic and confidence-building measures. They played ridiculous games, canceling meetings because the Croatians wanted to bring five journalists instead of two and all sorts of insane and bizarre behaviours which indicated to us, the mediators, and, I have to say, to the Croatian government that they weren't serious. And when the time came following the signing of an economic and confidence-building measures to present a political plan, they refused to even receive this plan. And you, when you had an opportunity to help, provided no help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, when did you draw up that Z-4 plan? When was it first heard of?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we decided in the late summer of 1994 that the economic and confidence-building negotiations were going no place, that a dangerous situation was developing because the Croatian government was becoming very impatient, and that the best chance to avoid war was to jump ahead to the political stage and to prepare a plan which could be presented to both sides, not on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, not like the Contact Group plan for Bosnia, but as a basis of negotiation. And we wanted to demonstrate to the Serbian side just how much autonomy would be possible within Croatia, and that's why the document looked as it did. The drafting of the document began in late August or early September of 1994, and it was completed in January of 1995, although substantially completed in September, early October of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The plan was first heard of in January 1995, the plan that you were working on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean the plan was known to -- it was known to many people in September, October of 1994. It was the subject of considerable press comment in Croatia. It was known -- some of the ideas were known to the Croatian government, and for that matter also to the Krajina Serbs, before January of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to certain ideas from the plan, but when did the plan itself come to be known?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was known that there was a plan in this time, in the latter part of 1994. The plan itself was presented on the 30th of January, 1995, to President Tudjman and attempted to be presented to the Krajina Serb leadership that same day and attempted to be presented to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the 13th of January was when the plan was first presented to Tudjman; is that right? That was the first person it was handed to. This was in January 1995; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, but in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that because the talks on economic relations were not producing any results, you speeded up work on the Z-4 plan. Now, do you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remember that on the 30th of November, 1994, which means two months prior to the appearance of the Z-4 plan, the government of the Republika Srpska Krajina, at a meeting in Knin, unanimously adopted a package on an agreement on economic relations with Croatia, thereby, as stated by the prime minister, and let me correct the translation, there's constant reference to Nikolic here, but it's not Nikolic, it's Mikelic. It should say "Mikelic." That it showed once again quite unequivocally that it supported a policy of peace and cooperation with the international community. You know that the initiative for a normalisation of economic relations had come precisely from Borislav's Mikelic's government, which Belgrade supported fully and encouraged to proceed along that path. Later on, Owen and Stoltenberg joined in and there were several meetings between representatives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is too long for a question. Ambassador, I don't know if you can comment on anything that's been said by the accused so far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- it's an interesting history, but it ignores the fact, the basic facts, which are that the cease-fire agreement was concluded on the 30th of March. It was meant to be followed by a meeting two weeks later in the Russian embassy, the Krajina ought to start economic and confidence-building negotiations. The Krajina Serbs refused to show up. We tried to reschedule, I think in June, for Plitvice. They wouldn't allow the Plitvice meeting to take place because the Croatians wanted to bring five journalists. They engaged in all sorts of antics and it was as a result of that that we started the political process. It was well known that we were working on the Z-4 plan. The fact that, very late in the day, another six months having elapsed that they agreed to economic and confidence-building measures which they only partially implemented, I don't see the significance of it. The fact is the only way to avoid war was to come to a political settlement. The patience of the Croatians had run out, and these games absolutely made the situation much worse. We tried our best to come to a solution, and the defendant, who had a decisive role -- decisive influence over these people refused to cooperate. Not only refused to cooperate, but according to several of the Krajina Serb leadership, ordered them not to accept the Z-4 plan. And the consequence was a war and 180.000 Serb refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know according to whose words, and that's very vague, and furthermore, it is not true, but let us proceed with the facts only, Mr. Galbraith. Do you know that even though you said that they avoided these meetings that the Assembly of the Republika Srpska Krajina in Knin adopted the texts of the agreement on mutual economic relations and cooperation between the RSK and the Republic of Croatia, and the documents were signed by Hrvoje Sarinic and Borislav Mikelic? This was at the end of 1994. So, first of all, the government that agreed, as I quoted, and after that the Assembly, as well. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I'm aware of it. In fact, I also signed as a witness those documents. But let me again say the relevant point is that they played games for six months. They brought the situation closer to war. The agreement came far too late and we saw that time was of the essence and which is why we felt it was very important to move forward with the political process, and that's what we attempted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Galbraith, let us clear up just a matter of detail. What I'm quoting from occurred even before the Z-4 plan appeared, so there were no gains. At the Assembly of the Republic of Srpska Krajina on the 1st of December 1994 accepted this agreement. And you also have here the fact that on the 11th of January, 1995, again before you had even presented the plan to Tudjman at the UNPROFOR base at the Zagreb airport Pleso, another round of delegations started on the implementation of the agreement on economic matters signed the previous month between the RSK and Croatia. It says that the talks were behind closed doors and that participating were international mediators Lord Owen and Stoltenberg. Heading the Krajina negotiating team was Borislav Mikelic and the Croatian Hrvoje Sarinic. So all this happened before you came out with the Z-4 plan. Therefore, something that happen afterwards cannot provoke something that occurred previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean. What are you trying to get across, because it's not clear. What is it you're trying to put to the witness? That you had no influence on this? Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point, Mr. May, is that these negotiations on economic relations and cooperation and confidence-building were continuing and developing in relations between the Croatian government and Knin with the mediation of Owen and Stoltenberg before the Z-4 plan was produced, that things were evolving according to their own dynamics and there was no alarm sounded that a war had to be engaged in between the Serbs in Krajina. That is the point, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the facts speak for themselves, Your Honour. There was a war and it was catastrophic, and the war was avoidable. It could have been avoided, absolutely could have been avoided had there been serious negotiations on a political settlement within Croatia. An incidently, it is absurd to say that things were progressing happily in November, December, January, 1994/1995. In January of 1995, the Croatians announced they weren't going to extend the UNPROFOR mandate beyond the 31st of March. They were going to force the UN to withdraw, which of course would have set up the situation for military action. Now, if they were so happy with everything, it would seem very surprising that they would take this action. There was a series of events that were escalating toward war. I could describe them in great detail, but they certainly included what I call the first Bihac crisis. November 12th of 1994, a series of attacks on Bihac. The end of the UNPROFOR mandate and a number of other steps that were driving toward war and the war actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, wasn't perhaps everything quite the opposite, that these things that I have mentioned as facts which you cannot deny pointed to the fact that a peaceful solution would be achieved through this dynamic process which was becoming increasingly intensive, and that the Croatian leadership really had no interest in a peaceful solution because they wouldn't have been able to expel 250.000 Serbs if there had been a peaceful solution? Isn't that right, Mr. Galbraith, or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that the president of Croatia was -- was prepared and did accept the document that had been prepared by the United States of America, not an insignificant country in the world, the European Union, Russia, and the United Nations. Milan Martic and his colleagues in Knin literally refused to accept this document. And you refused to see the representatives of these countries. Now, I don't see how that behaviour can be said by anybody to be conducive to peace or part of any process that had momentum toward peace. I don't understand it, and I don't think it's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you challenge that you refused to see this emissary then you should put it to the witness, if you challenge that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I challenge it. And secondly, Mr. Galbraith was not in Belgrade at all. He was the ambassador in Croatia, and I received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it's the charges d'affaires who he says you refused to see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, never -- this time there's reference to Rudy Perina, who was charges d'affaires in Yugoslavia. I never refused to receive him as I never refused to receive Ambassador Roberts. That is completely untrue. But let us move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We'll deal with that and find out what the source of information which the witness has as to the refusal to see the charges d'affaires.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're discussing two separate events so, I want to be clear about that. The first event was in January of 1995 when the Z-4 representatives requested an appointment to see Mr. Milosevic. Indeed, I would have been the representative who would have gone and seen him along with Ambassador Ahrens, who was the German representative. He was not a bilateral ambassador in Croatia. I was dual-hatted at that time. An Ambassador Matakota [phoen] who represented the United Nations, and the Russian ambassador. We were told by Lord Owen, and confirmed by the American Embassy in Belgrade, that Mr. Milosevic had turned down the request to see us. This had been transmitted in the way in which these are a formal request to see him to present the plan. That was the event in January of 1995. In August of 1995, this was August 2nd, this was the meeting I had in Belgrade with Babic which produced the last-minute agreement to try to head off the war. The next day Rudy Perina requested an appointment to see Mr. Milosevic to demarche him to support the Galbraith-Babic agreement. He refused to see Mr. Perina that day, the 3rd of August, and the next day the Croatian army attacked the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, I never refused to receive Rudy Perina. I wasn't in Belgrade at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's no use repeating that. You've heard what the witness says. If you can give evidence about it, no doubt you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can point out, even if the witness were not in Belgrade, which I don't know, there are telephones, and we did use telephones to talk to leaders on urgent matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why then didn't they speak to me by telephone? They didn't want to talk to me, Mr. Galbraith. Why don't you say that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We desperately wanted to talk to you. We desperately wanted you to support this last-minute agreement. We desperately wanted to head off the war. Mr. Babic also wanted to see you and get you to support this last-minute agreement. As he said to me, one sentence from you and Knin would have agreed, and I think there would have been a very good chance at that point that Operation Storm, even at that last minute, Operation Storm could have been headed off and a 180.000 Serbs from the Krajina would not have been driven from their homes and a huge humanitarian catastrophe would not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, Babic testified here. He asked to see me. He heard that I wasn't in Belgrade. He asked for my telephone from people from the Ministry of the Interior, and my telephone was known to all my associates always. I was on vacation. He reached me by phone. He even explained here that it could be seen that I was from a distance. The line was not good because I was on a mountain. And the only thing he said to me is that he had accepted the Z-4 plan. And he testified here, I can't remember the whole conversation myself, but he said that I just said, yes, yes, peacefully. And that is what he testified about here. There was no mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't possibly comment on what Mr. Babic had said. During the adjournment, Mr. Nice, would you please check what Babic said about this so we may have it for the record, and the witness can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I checked that yesterday. I have it all ready if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So no one, even Babic, according to his own testimony, and of course everyone else knows this too, never mentioned to the officials of Serbia that he spoke to and from whom he asked for my telephone number, he never mentioned any kind of threat of war, nor did anyone imagine that there could be a war or an invasion or any such thing as the Storm operation as a result of which the Serbs were thrown out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... on what Mr. Babic may or may not have said here, and we'll check it after the adjournment. Your information, please, Ambassador, what was your information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, I don't -- Mr. Milosevic must have been very cut off on top of the mountain, because everybody else in the world understood that in August 1995, Europe was on the verge of the biggest battle since the Second World War. And how any leader, any responsible leader could be on vacation with all this happening and with the fate of so many people, may I add, so many Serbs, at stake, I cannot understand. But, you know, it was clear that the Croatians were going to attack. It was in the press. It was -- their forces were mobilised. I mean, he could not have not known this. And so -- I mean, what else can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Judging by what we learned here, Mr. Galbraith, it appears that the only person who was well-informed about this was Milan Babic, who even according to his own testimony, doesn't say that he informed anyone. No one expect that had Croatia could attack areas under the protection of the United Nations. Truly no one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered. What he said was that everybody knew, and that must have included you. That's what he says. Now, that may be a matter which we will have to determine in due course as to whether you did or you didn't know. But let us move on. In fact, it's time for an adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In case the Chamber has any time to do research over the break, it's, I think, page 13265. 13265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you can tell us what it says. Please summarise it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Kwon has found what seems to be the relevant passage. It says he was in touch with Milosevic and what did he say? "He repeated, he mumbled as if he was speaking out of a dream. He just said, yes, yes, slowly, slowly, everything would be conducted calmly. Those were his words over the phone. And he said, 'Contact Vlatko Jovanovic. Consult him.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: , but in fairness to the accused one has to look on because this was subject -- this was during examination-in-chief. The accused suggested that the interpretation of the word "mirno" was incorrect and I think it should have been either slowly or calmly. And on the following page, the witness said calmly or peacefully. And if I may very briefly put that in the setting of the other points that the accused is raising, the Chamber may be assisted by recalling that the witness Babic did speak of an April 1995 conversation with the accused where the accused had referred to Z-4 as a good plan, although the witness didn't believe that -- didn't believe what Milosevic was saying to him about that and never mentioned it to Galbraith, to the witness, Ambassador Galbraith. And Babic also dealt with Exhibit 352, 104, the capable, the United Kingdom cable which sets out how he had -- he, Babic, had been refused access by the accused, in paragraph 6, and it appears he confirms that. So that the sequence of events would be apart from the April 1995 contact, which was not communicated to Ambassador Galbraith would be on Babic's evidence refusal to see him, Babic, followed by the phone call organised by Stanisic and Babic not informing Ambassador Galbraith that he'd had the phone call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And also for the fairness of the accused, I have to not that to the answer asked by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, "Did you actually have an ultimatum from Mr. Galbraith to accept the plan right now, otherwise, consequences would happen?" Mr. Babic answered, he said: "What we could expect if we didn't accept, which meant a Croatian aggression and that we could fare the same as Western Slavonia." And the page number, in hard copy, starts from 13256, not 265. If you have any comment, Ambassador. Yes. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've got three-quarters of an hour more with this witness if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not sufficient for me, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have adjudged it sufficient. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Kwon said a minute ago had to do with the conversation between this witness and Mr. Babic, and as you may recall, during his testimony, he did not say a single word, nor did he mention to me that there was any danger of any kind of attack against Krajina, and you will see that in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Secondly, this correction that Mr. May explained, not very well, Babic said that his answer to my information that he had talked to Galbraith and that he had accepted the Z-4 plan was, "Yes, yes. Calmly, calmly." It did not mean "slowly," it meant "calmly." Calm is a very clear word, calmly, in the sense of peaceably. I'm talking about a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The matter has been put to the witness. He has no comment. It's the evidence of another witness. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will fully agree with you, Mr. Galbraith, that it would have been totally irresponsible for me to be sitting vacationing somewhere, on top of a mountain, while a war was in the making. No one in Serbia, Mr. Galbraith, knew or could have supposed that Croatia would attack UN protected areas. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry. Let the witness deal with that assertion. Ambassador, you said that everybody knew, using a colloquialism, that Croatia was likely to attack. What were the objective signs of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian military was fully mobilised. They were positioned at the boundaries of the Krajina region. There was a huge amount of press coverage of the impending war. There were statements by Croatian officials that while they didn't necessarily directly say war would come tomorrow that in every way indicated that war was imminent. There was warnings from UN officials, and there was the warnings that I conveyed to Mr. Babic, that I conveyed to UN officials or conversations I had with UN officials and through them conveyed to the leadership in Knin. There was absolutely no secret about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously it was not a secret to Babic, but Babic did not convey this secret to anybody else. Do you find that clear at least?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness is saying, so you understand it, is that it was plain from press coverage and mobilisation that a war was likely. Now, it wasn't a question -- you misrepresent him when you say it was just a matter of Babic. He's saying that it was clear to everybody at the time. Now, that's the point that he makes. If you want to challenge that, of course you can, saying nobody knew.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I'm challenging that, because in Serbia, nobody could have supposed that. It seems to that we are responsible for the fact that we did not assume that Croatia could attack an UN protected area. As a matter of fact, at the time when negotiations were scheduled in Geneva between the representatives of the Republic of Srpska Krajina and the Republic of Croatia, Yugoslavia or Serbia were not invited there, of course, because this was a matter between Zagreb and Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Galbraith, these are UN protected areas. There is no doubt about that. Negotiations in Geneva were scheduled precisely for that time between the representatives of the republic of Srpska Krajina, and the Republic of Croatia, and you claim that we should have assumed that Croatian forces would attack a UN protected area at the point in time when negotiations were scheduled between them and Knin. Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Croatian army had taken over an UN protected area at the beginning of May, 1995, just three months before these events. So I can't understand your statement saying that it was unthinkable that this could happen. It in fact had just happened in UN protected area Sector West just three months before. As to the meetings in Geneva, they -- the Croatians used them as a vehicle to present their final ultimatum. They anticipated that there would not be a positive answer, and they proceeded with their attack. I don't think the Croatians had the slightest thought that there were going to be meaningful negotiations. And it was clear to me as it was to other diplomats in Zagreb, and I think to the broader international community, that this meeting in Geneva was just that, that it was pro forma, that it was a very dangerous situation, that the -- that Tudjman was going to outline demands that he had already stated, that the Serbs were going to refuse them and that that would provide the pretext for a war. I would also suggest that one can go back and look at what was in the press in the first few days of August of 1995. I think it would be inescapable that there was this looming crisis and a very strong likelihood of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, you've just given an argument against what you've been asserting, because it is correct that the aggression on the 1st and 2nd of May against Western Slavonia did occur. This was an aggression against a UN protected area, but it had been condemned by the UN, and Croatia had been warned that such violations were not to happen. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had been opposed by the United Nations. There had been no practical adverse consequences, and by July of 1995, Croatia and Bosnia were in a state of acute crisis created by the activities of General Ratko Mladic and the Bosnian Serbs who had taken UNPROFOR personnel as hostage, who had taken over the enclave of Srebrenica, massacred the 7.000 men and boys, who attacked Zepa, another UN protected area, had taken that over and were in the process of attacking Bihac. Meanwhile, the Croatian army was marching up the Livno Valley and making considerable progress. The war was heating up in an extraordinary way at that point in time. And I think any observer, any knowledgeable observer, would have realised -- and knowledgeable observers all did realise that there was a very strong likelihood of a further escalation. I think they also saw that the United States and the other members of international community were extremely concerned about what was happening, that indeed we saw this as a major crisis. Our policies were in crisis. And to have -- well, I don't think that anybody could have assumed that the posture of the international community would be the same toward a possible Croatian military action in August of 1995 as it had been for example in 1994 when the first Bihac crisis took place. And in any event, one could only have observed the relatively tepid response of the international community to the Croatian takeover of Sector West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution at a later state can produce some Serbian newspapers dealing with this issue and how it was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's already on my list of things to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would be pleased to see that because in Serbia nobody had assumed that. But from this vantage point, Mr. Galbraith, it's quite clear that Croatia dared attack Krajina with your permission. When I say "your permission," I'm not saying you personally. I'm talking about the permission given by your country. And not only with your permission but also with the active cooperation of your representatives, of your instructors in the attack against the Krajina. Of course, nobody knew about that either. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've described the position of the United States yesterday, and I'll repeat that. Our position was we neither opposed nor endorsed Croatian military action. We did warn -- I personally, on instructions, warned President Tudjman that military action was inherently risky, that if he ran into difficulty he could count on no help from the United States, and that there would be serious consequences to US-Croatia relations if there were attacks on civilians or on UN personnel. And I might add parenthetically, indeed because Croatia failed to respect the Serbian -- the property of the Serbian civilians and tolerated the killing the stragglers, there were serious consequences for US-Croatia relations. Now, to the second part of your question, the United States did not assist the Croatian military in this operation. To the best of my knowledge it provided no instruction to the Croatians on any aspect of the military operation in spite of some very imaginative press stories suggesting otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know very well that as far back as 1994, September 1994, an agreement was signed in Washington between the Minister of Defence of Croatia, Gojko Susak, and the US company MPRI. It was signed by the executive officer of that company and General Carl Vaughan. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that organisation practically planned this operation and participated in this Operation Storm, supporting the Croatian initiative against an UN protected area, and you consider that to be legal; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far as I know, the company did not plan any aspect of Operation Storm. It did not participate in any aspect of Operation Storm. Its contract was not in any way related to that kind of military planning. If it had done so -- if it did so, it did so without the authorisation of the United States government, and I believe it would have also been in violation of the United States law. At that time, there was an embargo on military assistance to the parties, and the United States on -- the United States itself honoured that embargo. It was -- among the things that MPRI was providing was human rights training and training in such areas as budgeting and sort of general leadership skills, and those were judged to be legal under US law and not a violation of UN Security Council Resolution 713.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on, just one thing, please. Since you said that you could not reach me, that Perina could not reach me, that Roberts could not reach me because I was away on vacation, if you already wanted to give this kind of information, why didn't you give it to the Foreign Minister, the Prime Minister, anybody, or why didn't you request telephone contact with me? It was possible at any time.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
