utterances.text: It was for -- referring now to the August meeting or August 3rd events, it was for the charges of the United States to try to get in contact with you. He attempted to get in contact with you. I don't know the particulars of it. Some of these officials the United States did not see because we did not recognise the government of -- of the so-called Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. Perina contacted the Foreign Minister, Jovanovic, and many others. So if you really cared about this, if you really wanted to convey some information or a demarche, are you trying to say that the US charges d'affaires could not deliver this at my office and would he not have known that I would have gotten it immediately for sure, or couldn't he have requested to speak to me on the telephone? He didn't ask for any such thing. He just asked for me to receive him and the answer given to him was I was not in Belgrade and that was it. There's a saying in Serbia, Mr. Galbraith, and it says that a person requests something and prays to God not to get it. So I think that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've exhausted this topic, but if you want to reply, Ambassador, you may and then we must move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is nonsense. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We desperately tried to avoid this war. We embarked on this initiative. Even at the very last minute we tried to get you to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. support it. We believed your public support could have headed off the war. You were on vacation at the moment that the catastrophe was overtaking 180.000 Serbs in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, catastrophe that was being prepared secretly and that was carried out at the -- to the surprise of everyone in Serbia, including myself, and anybody, any ordinary citizen of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have exhausted this topic now. Will you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, is it correct that precisely this organisation of yours, this military organisation of yours, MPRI, had a programme at the Petar Zrinjski Officers School that started considerably before the attack on Krajina and just before the attack on the Srpska Krajina, and on the 17th of July, 1995, in Brioni, a seminar was held precisely for these top officials --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're misrepresenting the evidence. It's not the first time. This is not the witness's organisation. It's a private organisation. In you're going to ask questions about it, you can ask them separately. What is alleged is that it had -- this organisation had an officers' school, yes, a programme at the officers' school, no doubt in Croatia. Do you know anything about that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a private organisation, so I didn't, obviously, follow all of its activities, but it did organise some kind of seminar, which I think had been planned for sometime in advance, in July of 1995 for the Croatian military. This was on human rights issues and leadership issues, you know, techniques for effective leadership. It had, so far as I know, nothing to do with war planning of any kind, and of course after the -- I received some reports on it as this programme was going on from my defence attache, and after Operation Storm and with all these allegations, I went back and I checked, and so far as I was able to determine, and I believe this is correct, there was no military planning carried out by this organisation of any kind. And in any event, it's absurd to think that a handful of retired American army officers arriving in July of 1995 could have transformed the military situation in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you insist on this being a private organisation, do you believe that this private organisation which brought together 200 elite American generals, retired, in all fairness, could have done something that was contrary to the policy of the United States?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information to indicate that they violated United States law and/or United States policy. That is to say, I have no information to indicate that they assisted the Croatian government in any military planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did they consist of 200 generals, elite but retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They -- it was an organisation of retired military -- consisting primarily of retired US military. Certainly I can't imagine that it had 200 generals. That would be a very large number of generals. But it is -- it was and it is a private company, so I can't speak further to who it is that actually works for the company. I mean, I know who is the head of it and I know people who were in Croatia. I think there were about ten or 15 officers working in Croatia at various times, retired officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Galbraith. At that time, do you remember that there was an affair that had to do with your participation and the participation of the CIA and the Pentagon on the 28th of July, a Croatian newspaper, Slobodna Dalmacija, wrote about it. Do you recall that, the participation in Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us finish on that note then. You believe that nothing illegal was done when the UN protected area was attacked and that the objective was not to have a war and to have the Serbs expelled. The objective was to attain peace. Is that what you're asserting, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I'm asserting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, isn't it quite obvious that not -- it wasn't -- you didn't want peace nor did the Croatian government, because if you had peace, you wouldn't be able to implement your brutal aggression that ultimately came and the fact that 200.000 Serbs were expelled from Krajina. Isn't that right, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are again totally misrepresenting the evidence. I don't think that's worthy of a response, but if you want to, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will simply say, first, the United States government did everything possible for peace, and I think the testimony I've given to you, Your Honour, speaks to that. Second, the Croatian army had -- the Croatian government clearly had decided on war, and it was the actions of Ratko Mladic and the Krajina Serbs that -- backed by the defendant that gave the Croatian army the pretext to launch a war and created an environment in which it was very difficult for any of the major international powers to restrain the Croatians. Third, Croatia engaged in much illegal and criminal behaviour in the course of Operation Storm. That included the -- permitting the systematic burning of the homes and property of the Serbian population there after they had left. It included the killing of several hundred stragglers. It included efforts by Tudjman who was, in my view, a racist, to prevent Serbs who were citizens of Croatia to return to their homes. We criticised this repeatedly, strongly, this illegal and immoral behaviour. We tried to reverse it. We imposed sanctions on Croatia, and indeed we succeeded in reversing at least some parts of it, because the Croatian government eventually did agree that Serbs from the Krajina could return home and could recover their citizenship, and indeed the new government in Croatia has been encouraging Serbian citizens to return home. Also, in negotiating the Eastern Slavonia agreement, one of our top priorities was to enable the Serbian citizens of that region to remain as this area became part of Croatia, and I'm proud to say that that in fact happened. Indeed, it was the only time in the former Yugoslavia where territory changed hands from one party to the other and the people of the ethnic group which had lost control actually remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, as you in a way defined this operation you were talking about General Mladic and the events that took place in Bosnia as a pretext, one of the causes for the attack on Krajina. Could you please be so kind as to comment this, something I received yesterday, in fact, precisely from the opposite side, Mr. Nice, this piece of information. I have two copies of the document. I'm going to hand one over to you to take a look at. We can place it on the overhead projector. And tell me whether you know anything about it, please. My time is limited here, of course, but we will have an opportunity of looking through all the facts and putting each piece in its proper place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The document seems to be -- Mr. Nice, you can help us with it. Perhaps you'd better have a look at it yourself to see if you have any objection to it being put to the witness. It's a letter from you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me make a correction. I received it from the Registrar, but it was in fact signed by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's part of our standard Rule 68 process, providing information in accordance with our duty. It says nothing about reliability of or our belief in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. May I have it back, please? What is the point you want to make through this document, Mr. Milosevic, rather than putting it to the witness? And if necessary, the witness can see it, but what is the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to hear Mr. Galbraith's comments with respect to the assertion made that I mentioned otherwise here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, while they're taking a moment to have a look at the document, the gentlemen, Mr. May and the others, it says here: "The Prosecution has received the following information. [In English] Allegedly Alija Izetbegovic ordered that a meeting take place on 28 September, 1993, between Izetbegovic and nine leaders from the Srebrenica pocket." [Interpretation] Then it goes on to state who these people are. And then it says the following: "[Previous translation continues]... [In English] by UNPROFOR helicopter and brought to Sarajevo. The meeting took place in the Holiday Inn. Izetbegovic told the delegation that he ordered the meeting to advise those present that he wanted -- that he wanted to exchange Srebrenica for Vogosca. Izetbegovic stated that President Clinton had offered him to let the Chetniks into Srebrenica to kill 5.000 Muslims and then there would be international military intervention. Delegation stated that they would not back such a proposal. The source of this information believes that what was proposed in 1993 procured in 1995."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the piece of paper. The bottom. It needn't be put on the ELMO, shouldn't be put on the ELMO, but it can be shown to the witness. Just a moment. Mr. Galbraith, just look at that, if you would. The accused has read it out. We have no idea what the source of this information is. It's apparently some information described as information which has come from a source to the Prosecution. Maybe you know absolutely nothing about it at all. Have you heard of any such suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I don't know which part of this to comment on. I mean, it's almost hilarious. I find it completely unbelievable that President Izetbegovic would make such a statement, especially to the people from Srebrenica. And of course, I mean, nobody could imagine that that President Clinton could offer to let the Chetniks go into Srebrenica to kill 5.000 people. I mean, it's just completely absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Chetniks are Izetbegovic's expression meaning the Serbs. So when he says Chetniks, that's what he means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear from the Prosecution about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just repeat so there will be no confusion about it that our duty to provide information coming to us that would qualify as Rule 68 reflects no attribution of credibility to the material and indeed we may all too easily be subject to intentional disinformation coming our way. We simply have a duty once information could qualify as Rule 68 material to make it available, but those viewing these proceedings must understand the material is handed over with absolutely no truth value being associated with it so far as we're concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just say as somebody who has followed the events in the former Yugoslavia for many years, this is obviously and patently absurd, and -- so would clearly fall in the category of disinformation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that we shall require the source of this information to be able to make some sort of judgement about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can deal with that later as a procedural issue in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. You can consider it. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. The piece of paper should be returned to the accused. Not be exhibited, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I hope this will not be difficult, because there are many names mentioned here, many names of people who were present at the meeting. So they have been identified, all those present. If not all of this them, then most of them so it won't be difficult to check that out. But let's go back to what you saying a moment ago about the crimes committed by the Croatian forces in Krajina. So without a doubt, many crimes were committed against the Serbs. Isn't that right, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that, and those crimes included the systematic destruction of the property of the Krajina Serbs. It included permitting the killing of several hundred stragglers and preventing people from being able to return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were talking yesterday in explaining your interview to the BBC that it wasn't ethnic cleansing because the people had fled before any kind of paramilitaries entered. Now, do you happen to know that the people had fled in the face of the grenades and shelling? Knin was heavily shelled and so were the surrounding areas. Or do you think they just escaped and fled just like that because they feared the Croatian army which was nearby? I'm sure you will remember that the attack began precisely with the heavy shelling of Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that people fled the shelling, and I'm sure that people fled because they feared the Croatian army. The shelling was relatively brief because there was effective no resistance. I think Knin fell within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you're claiming that it -- it's not ethnic cleansing when you use shells to destroy a town and inhabitants have to flee, but you only consider it to be ethnic cleansing from the point that troops enter the town and start to slaughter the people and set fire to the houses? Is that the limit, is that the borderline where you differentiate what is and is not ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first point is that -- just a factual matter. Knin was not destroyed. In fact, it was not all that heavily damaged. I had embassy officers in there within a few days of the Croatian takeover. Second, as to what constitutes ethnic cleansing, I would say that it is a combination of -- and the important word here is the "combination" of military actions, certainly can include shelling. It includes the entry of troops into the territory -- into a village, but it also includes when the people are there executions, beatings, torture, you know, burning of houses, rape, activities intending to terrorise the population and force them to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, did all of this actually take place, Mr. Galbraith? Did it happen, all that together, all the things that you enumerated taken together, did they happen?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they happened in Croatia. Did they happen in Operation Storm? No, because the population had -- almost all of it had already left before the Croatian military entered the towns and, therefore, there were basically no people there for them to terrorise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the ones who stayed on, the stragglers, they were killed. Is that right, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Several hundred of the stragglers were killed, and it was a very serious crime. These were, in some cases, old people who -- in isolated farmhouses, who were too sick or too infirm to leave. Unspeakable crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Galbraith. Now, do you remember that on the 28th of July, 1995, Croatia with its troops stormed Glamoc and Grahovo? Otherwise, it was the celebration of the 50th anniversary of the Serb people against the Ustasha state. Now, do you happen to know that this storming was preceded by Tudjman's and Izetbegovic's agreement to send reinforcements? The agreement was made in Split, and I think you attended. Isn't that right, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was preceded by a summit between Tudjman and Izetbegovic which was held in Split and which I attended, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right then. Now, do you consider yourself and the United States government responsible for the crimes that were committed against the Serbs? A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to answer that. That's a preposterous question. You've heard it, you've heard what the witnesses has said. Now, you've got one minute left, so you better have your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm very sorry that I really don't have the time to cross-examine the witness fully. That has become customary here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me, Mr. Galbraith, as you spent five years in Zagreb, according to what Chris Hedges from The New York Times 1997 says, who wrote a text on the 24th of December, 1997, you have a special place because you did not represent the true state of affairs to Washington and the relationship of the Serbian authorities until the Serbs were expelled -- were actually expelled from Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And tell me this then, John Galvin, the retired general who took part in the negotiations in Yugoslavia together with Charles Redman who was otherwise an expert for the so-called doctrine of low-intensity conflicts was an advisor to Alija Izetbegovic, a military advisor to boot; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Charles Redman? He was a US ambassador and the American representative to the Contact Group. And I don't think he was an expert on low-intensity conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this then, please, is it true and correct that for the Iranian shipments of weapons to Bosnia-Herzegovina that your president knew about that, Bill Clinton, and that Holbrooke, in his testimony to Congress, recognised that arms were being infiltrated into Croatia from Iran?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is your last question. Your time is then up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true and generally well known that you were included in the affair over the secret import and smuggling of arms into Bosnia? You were involved in that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, I was not involved in the -- in any way in the smuggling of arms into Bosnia. This was the subject -- this whole issue was the subject of a number of congressional hearings and reports, as well as a lot of press discussion, and what I did came out in the course of that and it was very simple. On the -- I think it was the 28th of April, 1994, President Tudjman asked me, as I knew he would, what would be the attitude of the United States if Croatia -- if Croatia were to accede to the request from Bosnia and Herzegovina to permit arms from Iran and from other countries to transit Croatia to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I told him, on instructions, of course, that I had no instructions, which he understood to mean that the United States did not object and indeed the arms went -- shipments went forward. Just a word of explanation, which is that the Clinton administration did not support UN Security Council Resolution 713. It thought that the arms embargo had favoured the aggressor because the aggressor, Serbia and its allies in Croatia and Bosnia, had basically had all the arms of the former JNA and that the victims, notably the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was essentially left undefended. The United States itself did not violate the arms embargo at any time. On the other hand, we took the position that Resolution 713 should not be the only UN Security Council Resolution should be honoured when every over one was being dishonoured mostly by the Serbian side including resolutions that required the protection of innocent civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That concludes your cross-examination. The transcript should be corrected to reflect that in my last intervention I characterised the witness's -- the accused's question as preposterous. It was not reflected in the transcript. It should be. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Galbraith, I should like to ask you some questions about facts, documents for which I assume you either know about, know what their contents are or should have had reason to know. If I understood you correctly yesterday, and I took a look at the transcript, you said that the process around -- surrounding plan Z-4 began on the 23rd of March, 1994, and lasted until sometime around Operation Storm and that it evolved in three stages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have here a report dated the 29th of March, 1994, which I was given by the OTP pursuant to Rule 68, and it has to do with the daily report of the observer mission of the European Union of the 29th of March, 1994. Can we agree that that was just a few days after this process over the Z-4 plan had started, when it was launched?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't the process of the Z-4 plan, but it was the -- the process in which Russia and the United States married up with the ICFY co-chairman in the Croatia peace process. But at that stage, we hadn't thought about preparing what became known as the Z-4 political plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the document available should the witness want to look at it, and I understand he has in any event been in a position to review it before giving evidence, so he knows about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wonder if actually I could see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a sufficient number of copies for Your Honours if you would like to have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is in this: First of all, point 2(A) at the beginning. That's something you already stated. It says, "the USA ambassador to Croatia, Peter Galbraith, said that the USA and Russia agreed that the reintegration of Krajina into Croatia must take place peacefully and that the Serbs should be given considerable autonomy." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, this "considerable autonomy," Mr. Ambassador, at that point in time after the preparations were launched for covering up this plan, the Z-4 plan, does that imply autonomy within those frameworks or perhaps in some other frameworks?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it was my view that any settlement that was mutually agreeable to the government of Croatia and to the Krajina Serbs that would preserve the territorial integrity of Croatia, enabled displaced Croatians to return home and ensured that the Serbian population could safely remain, that any such settlement would be agreeable to me, and I know it would have been agreeable to the United States. So I don't think -- we were not committed to any particular framework. We were committed to a peace settlement that adhered to certain fundamental principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's how I understood it too. However, this Z-4 plan was prepared already in September, and as we heard yesterday, you spoke about that, that you presented it for the first time to the leaders of Srpska Krajina and also to President Tudjman. That's how I understand it yesterday. And that was on the 30th of January, 1995; is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan was substantially prepared in September and October of 1995. It wasn't finalised until January -- sorry, September and October of 1994. It was not finalised until January of 1995. Otherwise, your statement about it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So during that first meeting when you offered up the plan to Martic and Abdic and Mikelic, you were given a relative answer, if I can put it that way. And Mr. Abdic said he was sorry because of that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was in my view nothing relative about the answer. The answer that they refused to receive the plan. I mean, Martic literally refused to pick the plan off the table when it was handed to him. I mean, it was -- it was the most -- it was the strongest possible objection, and it was intentionally insulting to the United States, to Russia, and to the European Union.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, the transcript says it was Mr. Abdic who said he was sorry. Is that right? I think it should be Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was Mr. Babic who said he was sorry. And it was Martic who refused to pick up the plan, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I should add to clarify: Babic said this privately to me as an aside. It in no way represented the decision of the collective leadership of the Krajina Serbs. It was just that he was, I think, obviously embarrassed by what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Galbraith, but I have here in my hands something that I also received from the Prosecution, a special report from the observer mission of the European Union in connection with the plan Z-4 dated the 31st of January, 1995. I have sufficient copies, one for you as well. Would you be kind enough to look at it. It is RO2358335834. And the following can be found in this text. The 31st of January, 1995, a day after the meeting with the gentlemen you spoke is to, and it says and I quote: "Ambassador Galbraith admitted that the Z-4 plan had been presented earlier than expected because of President Tudjman's insistence that the negotiations be speeded up." Is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- no. I don't think that that report accurately reflects my thinking or what I said. I believe that the Z-4 plan was presented too late, and indeed --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, I'm just asking whether you said that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could I have a copy of that document together with that of 29th of March. For the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell Their Honours whether what is stated here in the special report of the European Union mission was written accurately. Does it correspond to what you said or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I don't believe the statement is -- accurately reflects my views, and therefore, I don't think it accurately reflects what I would have said. I think it's quite likely that I said that there was -- that because of -- that there was a lot of pressure on us to go forward with the negotiations as a result of President Tudjman's action in -- in terminating the -- announcing the termination of the UNPROFOR mandate and because I felt that we were -- that this was a situation that was headed toward. But I don't think I would have said, because it wouldn't have been right, that the Z-4 plan was presented too soon. I mean, on the contrary, my view is that it was presented too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in that same report, one finds the following, that the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Babic, in a recent statement, said, "Regarding the status offered to the RSK, that the people of the republic should decide." There is no mention of the fact that he said he was sorry. But on the contrary, it says that he said that such a plan could not be accepted unless the people of the Serbian Krajina were able to take a stand about it. Does that correspond to the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if your question is is it true that Foreign Minister Babic in a recent statement said the future status of the RSK must be decided by the population of the RSK, I have no reason to doubt that he might have said that in a recent statement. I would note that the document you've presented to me also points out that -- correctly that Dr. Babic, in a discreet meeting the last week had been more forth coming. And it also says in paragraph 7 an initial opinion from very limited interviews with RSK citizens is that some form of highly independent autonomy for the quote unquote RSK albeit within Croatia might very reluctantly be considered better than continued hostility, isolation, and poverty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The very next day, you had a meeting with Mr. Tudjman in the morning, and as I heard from you yesterday, could you please explain to Their Honours the following: Tudjman stated that he agreed that negotiations be conducted within that framework but he did so reluctantly. And later on, there was no chance to test Croatia's position precisely because the rejection by the Serbs. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that you said that you had in mind an autonomy which should lead to peace, in that period of time from the 23rd of March until the 4th of August, 23rd of March, 1994, until the 4th of August, 1995, did Croatia, or, rather, President Tudjman ever present their own views as to how they envisaged the autonomy of the Republic of Srpska Krajina within Croatia? Was ever any such proposal presented by them?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In what form?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were autonomy provisions contained within the Croatian constitutional law, and in fact they were not -- also not unsubstantial. Obviously much less than was in the Z-4 plan, but there was a fair amount of autonomy contained in the Croatian constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your excellency, Ambassador Galbraith, I'm very familiar with all those conditions that were in force at the time and are now. I'm asking whether there was any kind of formal offer in the form of a document or not.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on numerous occasions the Croatian -- President Tudjman and his principal colleagues said, you know, pointed to the Croatian constitutional law, which is of course a document, and said, you know, this is a basis for a settlement. I believe they indicated that it might even be in some parts negotiable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in this document dated the 29th of March, it also says in paragraph 2A/2, the following: The Yugoslav leadership obviously, and this is a comment by a mission of the European Union, is also bringing pressure to bear on the Krajina that it sign the agreement because for the FRY, this is the only way to ensure a lifting of the sanctions on Serbia and Montenegro. Is that right, that is that the European mission had information of this kind that it was in the interest of Yugoslavia, that is of Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're now referring to the document of the 29th of March of 1994, which I no longer have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I speak for myself, but I'd be grateful if you would finish by the adjournment, please, if you could adjust the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour, but I have another two documents which I feel that Your Honours should have access to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let us try and speed it along. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, I have no reason to doubt the accuracy of this statement that the Yugoslav leadership is pressing the Krajina to sign the cease-fire agreement, which is the operative agreement, but that has nothing to do with the political plan. This was a very limited ceasefire agreement that created zones of separation and regulated a number of police that might be in these zones and those kind of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, I have no right to debate this with. I just asked you. But I would like to ask also, this whole period from the 29th of March until the 4th of August, 1994, did the European mission have any information that would say or show that the position of Yugoslavia was not what it says here? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, I can't speak to what information the European Union mission might have. The United States is not a member of the European Union and, therefore, of its mission. But I would -- I mean, I would think that the statement contained in here is true and remained true, namely that the Yugoslav leadership wanted the Krajina government to sign and I suppose honour the cease-fire agreement. Again, that has nothing to do with -- or very little to do with the big issue which was to have a political settlement within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to ask you to look at another document I have, a special report of the European Union regarding the positions taken at the Geneva negotiations in -- on the 3rd of August, 1995. I have a copy for you, and I have copies for Their Honours as well. This is what it says in the summary at the very beginning: "After talks in Belgrade with the ambassador of the United States in Croatia on the 2nd of August, 1995, the new Prime Minister of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, Dr. Babic, sent a Krajina delegation to talks in Geneva on the 3rd of August, 1995, to accept the Z-4 plan as a basis for negotiations with Croatia. And then it goes on to say: "That same day he declared that Serbia's president, Milosevic, supported the idea on negotiations based on the Z-4 plan." And then further on, it also says: "On the 3rd of August, the new prime minister of RSK, Milan Babic, declared that the Serbs were ready to initiate political negotiations with Zagreb on the basis after modified and improved Z-4 plan. He confirmed that on the 2nd of August he met in Belgrade with the US Ambassador in Croatia, Mr. Galbraith, who promised that the United States would try to dissuade Croatia from attacking Krajina." Are you aware of this report and that the observer mission of the European Union already had information conveyed by Mr. Babic that Milosevic agreed with the Z-4 plan?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the negotiators in Geneva had a clear sign and evidence that Mr. Milosevic supported and accepted the Z-4 plan before the negotiations on a peaceful settlement were due to begin?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, the ECMM was not one of the negotiators in Geneva. Second, Mr. Milosevic did not support these negotiations based on the Z-4 plan or based on the reintegration of the Krajina into Croatia. He made no attempt to -- to support the idea, at least none that was sufficient to be impressive on Tudjman, he made no public statement. I mean I'm not privy to the call that he had with Babic, but from the testimony that I have heard, even that hardly counts as a -- as a -- as any kind of endorsement or any kind of strong endorsement. What was required was for Milosevic to come out and strongly and unequivocally endorse a political settlement within Croatia, and that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may complete this part of my examination before the break. Two more points. Surely the most important thing is that the ECMM had this information and that after that, the Serbian delegation and the documents indicates what the agreement looked like, the Serbian delegation signed it and accepted the Z-4 plan. Surely that is the most important thing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what it says here is not that. It says that the Serbian delegation accepted the seven-point plan although they said they wanted to consult with Knin before agreeing officially. They created sufficient ambiguity that some of the international observers doubted that they had accepted it, and it provided a perfect pretext for the Croatians to say that the Serbian side had not fully accepted it. In any event, if I may remind the Court of what President Tudjman said to me. He said, you know -- he did not believe that Babic had sufficient clout actually to deliver, and what was missing clearly was the strong endorsements of Martic and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Galbraith, the Croats did not sign that agreement. Is that in dispute or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it is not in dispute. They did not sign the agreement, nor, I think, did the Serbs sign anything either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me now to read the last part of that report which is important in view of something that His Honour Judge Kwon referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we're going to adjourn now. Mr. Tapuskovic, I must ask you to try and speed things up. You've been cross-examining for half an hour. Of course you can have slightly more time, but please try and restrict it. Mr. Nice, we've got another witness waiting, have we.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have a 92 bis witness waiting who will be as long as basically cross-examination time takes because I should be only a few minutes with him and I've got a couple of administrative things to explain before we get there, but that...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had intended to read the entire text of the conclusions of the Special Rapporteur of the head of the ECMM, but I just wanted to check with you whether you would like these three documents to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit them into evidence with C numbers. Please do not read the entire text, because time is short. But if you want briefly to ask the witness something, you can. Yes, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, if the Prosecution could explain us as to the format of this document. This is not the original, and this seems to be Prosecution's documents summarising some other original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They are documents that we have, and you will see at the head of them we have them originally under certain terms. Those terms no longer apply. And as to the particular form, they are redacted to a degree. And they cannot be -- they cannot be changed in format from the present way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in connection with this last document, let me just note that in the conclusion it says that the Special Rapporteur established that on that day, that is the 3rd of August, 1995, at 1930 hours, on the most important news programme, the first item was that the Serbs had rejected a peaceful reintegration into Croatia. Are you aware of this news report that was broadcast that the Serbs had refused peaceful reintegration within Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document to which you refer. However, I am aware of that broadcast. And as I recall, it was preceded, maybe an hour or two earlier, by a more positive broadcast about my mission to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, just a couple of more questions in connection with this last issue. It has to do with the plan. You stated yesterday that on the 1st of August, at Brioni, you spoke to Tudjman about the problem having to do with Babic, that you wanted to meet with Babic as soon as possible. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a primary purpose of my mission to Brioni, but when I was at Brioni, I indicated that Babic wanted to meet with me and asked for Tudjman's views.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But you were add Brioni on the 31st of July, 1995, also; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there on the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I just have here in front of me your statement which you gave to the investigators on the 9th and 10th of December, 2002, and it says that on the 31st of July, 1995, you were at Brioni and that you advised them that if they embark upon the operation that they have to protect the civilian population. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had misrecollected the date, and the correct date was the 1st of August. I apologise for the error.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I also thought this was an error. But you were there on the 1st of August. Are you aware of a meeting that President Tudjman had with his generals and even officials on the 31st of July, the day prior to your visit? Were you aware of such a meeting taking place? If you were there on the 1st of August, did you know or not that Tudjman held a meeting with his generals at Brioni on the 31st of July, the day before your visit?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew on the 31st of July that such a meeting had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that meeting Tudjman told the generals present, I don't know whether he passed on this information to you, with regard to the Bihac problem the following: The situation now is such that representatives of the United Nations Akashi and Stoltenberg have taken this reason out of our hands," the reference is to Bihac, "because they're withdrawing their forces from Bihac now. They will not attack. They are allowing the UN CO to take positions there for monitoring, and clearly they have passed on this information to the whole world." Did you know that Tudjman said this, and are you aware of the move taken by Akashi and Stoltenberg to stop the Serbs and that they had agreed to this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of an UN effort to try to ease the situation around Bihac and to get monitors in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, I am quoting what Tudjman said at that meeting held on the 31st of July. These are the minutes of that meeting which I received from the Prosecution, and the date of the meeting was the 31st of July. And in those minutes or that report, you can also find - I don't know whether you were aware of this, maybe you learnt about it later, and I quote: "Therefore, we have no justification to embark upon the deblocking of Bihac. We have the inclination of the United States if, gentlemen, you decide to engage in that attack as you did in Slavonia." Do you know that he said that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that, or I know that he said something approximately like that, because I had an opportunity I think the day before yesterday to review those minutes. I did not know he had made such a statement at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he completed his statement by saying: "That is the purpose of this discussion today, to inflict such a blow on the Serbs that they should virtually disappear"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I saw those minutes two days ago. I was very much aware that Croatia was planning military action, which is precisely why I was so eager and so determined to try to find a peaceful settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. Do you know that he said that he had instructed Sarinic to go to the negotiations in Geneva but that should just be a smoke screen and that the acceptance of any kind of peace plan was absolutely out of the question?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any such statement at the time. Again, I have reviewed those minutes, and I think before I accepted everything that you said, I would want to look at them in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this the last document? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. This is the last document, Your Honour, Judge May. I really see no reason why we have this reaction. I really think this is a serious problem. I really think that you need to know this. Just interrupt me and I'll sit down if that is what you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you get on with it, Mr. Tapuskovic, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. I am doing my very best to make my questions very brief and Mr. Galbraith is entitled to speak at length at his will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last question is: Do you know that Boutros-Ghali on the 3rd of August called up President Tudjman and appealed to him not to engage in that attack. Are you aware of that? There is evidence of that but I'm asking you whether you knew about it. He was the Secretary-General of the UN at the time.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't now recall that he made such -- I do not now recall whether I was aware of such a call at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So far we have three documents. We'll exhibit them. If there's another one, we'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am giving you this document, the document in question. These are minutes from the meeting between Franjo Tudjman and his Supreme Commanders, and I'm handing it in. Thank you. The 31st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the special report from the observer mission from the European Union dated the 31st of January, 1995, is Chamber Exhibit 8. The daily report dated 29th of March 1994 is Chamber Exhibit 9. The special report of the head of the observer mission of the European Union dated the 3rd August 1995 is Chamber Exhibit 10, and the minutes I was just handed is Chamber Exhibit 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points arising from documents. I think in the minutes there's a reference to Bihac not being a pretext for war because of the Livno operation. Can you comment on that very briefly?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Croatians had undertaken a military operation going up the Livno Valley which had the effect of relieving some of the pressure on Bihac because the Bosnian Serb army had to redeploy forces to meet the threat that was coming from being posed by the Croatian army coming up the Livno Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In court Exhibit 9, the ECMM document of the 29th of March, there is one passage of all of the material put to you that is in contrast to your account where it suggests that the main obstacle to the agreement was the fact that the president of the RSK, Martic, backed by Milosevic and absolutely devoted to him, didn't have the majority of parliament, whereas what is described as hard-line Serbs led by Babic are opposing the idea. Can you give any explanation for why that report by the ECMM it's towards the bottom of the first page, is in contrast to your evidence and recollection?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not, I think, in contrast to my evidence or recollection. I said yesterday that in 1994, when this took place, that Babic was using these negotiations as a political club against Martic, but -- and as you know, I did not meet with Babic in 1994, but -- because he refused to meet with me. But in 1995, as the situation became more serious, war more imminent, it was my impression that he was much more open and more flexible to a political settlement. In other words, when the time came critical and the survival of the RSK or the Krajina Serbs was at stake, he recognised the reality and seemed prepared to make the kind of concessions that could possibly have averted a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Kwon raised the issue of contemporaneous newspaper reporting at the time of Storm. Do you know anything about contemporaneous newspaper reporting? Are you aware one way or the other of whether Belgrade reporting would have objectives to serve other than the mere dissemination of news?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not what could remotely be described as a free press in Belgrade at that time. So I -- the Belgrade press would have reflected what the Serbian government and what the defendant wanted it to say. When I refer to "newspaper reporting," I was referring to items that might have been appearing in the international press and, for that matter, in the Croatian press. I realise there were sanctions, but I am a hundred per cent confident that what was in the major newspapers of the world would actually have been picked up by officials in Serbia, by their intelligence agencies, and so forth. And if I might add, there was a Yugoslav representative in Zagreb at this time, and if he failed to pick up the signals about what was happening, then he would be one of the most incompetent diplomats on the face of the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it may be that not only Belgrade but Croatian or, indeed, even Knin newspapers are what we'll have to turn to guidance on this. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But on your last answer about intelligence the accused suggested really that he was ignorant of the impending attack. As far as you understood, did Belgrade have an intelligence capability that would have penetrated Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Substantial? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how substantial it would have been, but I know that they had a capability that was able to penetrate in Zagreb as the Croatians indeed had a capability of penetrating in Serbia. What I know the Court must be aware of is that after all this was all one country. These people all knew each other. There were lots of links, and whatever the level of penetration that the Serb intelligence agency had, again I'm confident that it would be sufficient to determine that there was a strong likelihood of military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think about three more questions. The first is this: We've seen in one of the documents some reference to Serbs leaving ahead of Operation Storm. Were you aware of that? If so, what significance do you attach to it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, and it is clear that at least some part of the Serbian population left on the orders of the leaders and not in response to the military action. It also, of course, suggests an awareness of the imminence of military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I can actually abandon my last two questions and leave it at that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you're not going to be able to ask any more questions. You know that. So what is the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that I will not be able to put any more questions, although I would have a great many to put, but the time will come for that. For the transcript, I just want to have a correction made. Something that was said and that is really not fair in terms of Martic's behaviour, and I understood the witness to say something different yesterday than what -- than the way it was interpreted during Mr. Tapuskovic's questioning. I just want to repeat this. Martic did not say that he would not look at the plan of Z-4. He said that he would not consider the plan until the problem of the UNPROFOR mandate is resolved. I think that that would be a comprehensive explanation. Not only the first part of the sentence. Is that right, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We can look at the transcript to see that. Ambassador, you've concluded your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the next witness who is a 92 bis witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with this, if I may interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We should since he is a 92 bis witness giving our ruling you asked us to give on timing, and the ruling we give is this: In relation to the Rule 92 bis witnesses, that is, witnesses whose statements are admitted under that Rule but who are tendered for cross-examination, the time allowed for cross-examination will normally be one hour. We have that in mind from our previous experience. When we started with one hour, we reduced it to three-quarters of an hour, but in the interests of allowing the accused further time, we will do so. It may be in the interests of justice to allow him slightly longer. So we will allow him one hour. But of course, circumstances may alter with the various witnesses and that ruling cannot be an absolute one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Grateful. Your Honour will know that we've provided a new list. I hope you have had an opportunity to see it because it will be coming in revised forms periodically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've seen it. I was not pleased to see that it seemed to be rather longer. I may be wrong, in comparison to the other list that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope will be pleased with its format. What I've done, intentionally, is to freeze the overall length of the list at what it was when we first started using it because familiar documents are more easy to handle if they remain familiar. It comes in four parts, and if one starts at the -- you may not have the document with you. No, it doesn't matter. The last two parts of the 92 bis listings, they, in each case, presuppose one hour total for a witness so that will have to be slightly extended but I hope by not very much on average. Part 2 is the list of witnesses who we won't be calling but will identify for you to know what's available in our category of witnesses we would like to call or you may find of interest to know what's available. At the end of the first part of the list and I'm very grateful to the team, particularly Ms. Wee and Ms. Dicklich who have done a great deal of work to get this in a most usable form. At the end of the first part of that list, 17, page 17 of 17, is an arithmetical compilation of the various component parts and it reveals how much we had to cut in order to finish on the time, because if we're the going to apply for any more time. And that is a lower figure than I feared at one stage. Now we've been able to put better estimates in. It's down to 38 days that we have to cut from the witnesses we would otherwise wish to call under lists 1, 3, and 4. And the reason the list is a bit longer is we're providing more detail at all times we hope to help you but we are shading out witnesses as they are called or otherwise rejected as no longer witnesses we wish to call, so that you can see as it were how well we've done so far, or how well the Court has done generally so far in getting through the evidence from what there is left, which is the ordinary black and white type. So I hope it's a very useful document, and it will come again probably in a month or thereabouts. We'll also provide a further fill-box document of the kind that you've been provided with periodically and you're due for an update before the summer recess for the Bosnia section which is an easy tool or a tool useful for showing what's outstanding to be proved and what has already be proved. I mentioned at an earlier stage that we might be converting these materials to a different computer system. I said I would discuss it with your staff in the event we didn't get round to having a joint meeting and I've made the decision independently of them. But although the new system will enable all of us, I hope, in due course to retrieve information, if we wish to, on a computer basis more readily. The system will also enables us to provide for you documents that are in the same format as you've had before in hard copy so that the familiarity of documents will continue. I think that's probably all I need to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whatever the new system will be I believe that the Prosecution is working on the index of Exhibit which I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That's very nearly ready. I think these documents actually all take a lot of time, and having got this one done and this one will now be much more easy to amend month by month so that we can get down to the final position, the exhibit list is on its way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That list should include, Mr. Nice, it seems to me, numbers for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the microphone. The list should include numbers for each exhibit. The reason being this: That at the moment, since we're using tabs, it's quite impossible to keep count the number of exhibits. I think for historical and other reasons we should have a number. Not the Court number, of course but merely the file number or whatever you call it in your document. So you start at 1, and then when you get to Exhibit 352 with 76 tabs, each one is a separate number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Well, we'll look into that. If the interest is in having a total number of exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- that can certainly be achieved as a comparatively small exercise. Whether we can do it as a running list on the same document, I don't know if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you can, whatever, we need to know precisely how many exhibits you've submitted and you should know too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, and my final observation on this list which I wanted to make is I've frozen the form of the list with numbers for witnesses on the second column. Your Honour is right to say that to some extent it's extended because where we've added names they've rather than change the numbers which makes it so confusing to refer to witnesses, they've gone in as A, B, C, and D numbers, but it's possible to see how many prospective witness there are left on the list quite easily, and in any event, because we need to reduce by 38 days the time that the witness will take, they're all not going to be called. That's quite obvious. And we'll carry on in the process of indicating by comment which ones are falling to the bottom of the list and which ones are witnesses we really must call. The next witness is a crime base witness. The general format for calling these witnesses under 92 bis as Your Honour will recall is that the witness, in this case it's a fully-open witness, has a 92 bis package which has been prepared. There may, as there will be in this witness's case, be a couple of additional exhibits, a map and a list of people killed. There will be a summary that I will read out which will be very brief, a minute or so. Some witnesses may at our application and if so granted add a couple of sentences before they are subject to cross-examination. This witness is Suad Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, please?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Suad Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, did you, here in the ICTY over recent days, go through your witness statement in the presence of an officer of the court, attest to its accuracy subject to corrections which were noted, and sign the documentation showing that you had attested your statement?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that be given an exhibit number

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 472.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, did you also mark a map which makes for ease of understanding your evidence --

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This will become Exhibit 366 -- 336, Suad Dzafic, and on that map, Mr. Dzafic, apart from villages that are highlighted is your village, your home village marked with a D or DJ?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, may this have a separate exhibit number. Is there a list prepared by you of those killed on the 21st of May of 1992 near Nova Kasaba in Vlasenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the list is Prosecution Exhibit 473.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's 21 names, and I think they're either most or all family connected to this witness most certainly. Your Honour, the summary of this witness's evidence is as follows: That he is from Vitkovici or from near Vitkovici in the Bratunac municipality. He returned from Serbia to his home village in that municipality in March 1992. He's able to give an account of the fate of himself and his fellow villagers, as his statement reveals, including by hearsay of the takeover of Bratunac town and other villages in the municipality in April and May of 1992. Krasno Polje, a neighbouring village, was attacked on the 10th of May, 1992, and on that day Serb neighbours of the witness came and told him and his fellow villagers that they would be safer if they fled to the woods, which they did, returning the same night. From that day and until the 18th of May, Serb police patrolled the village, but on the 17th of May the police chief came and asked them to hand in any weapons that they owned. On the morning of the following day, the 18th of May, Serb neighbours, now armed, surrounded the village. This witness with fellow villagers were put onto buses, transferred to Bratunac, and at about 3.00 on the afternoon, the buses left Bratunac and went to Vlasenica. Each bus had an armed guard on board. At Vlasenica they parked through the bus station, being surrounded by a mixed group of soldiers. The witness identifying some of the guards as being Arkan's Tigers and others as Beli Orlovi. The men of military age and five younger males were taken to the Vlasenica SUP where they were detained until the 21st of May, during which time they were beaten and maltreated. On that day the 21st of May, the men of military age were taken out of the SUP and put on a bus accompanied by an armoured vehicle which had been parked near the bus and which joined the bus on convoy along with four other cars, one of those cars having a skull on its door. Those vehicles left in the direction of Bratunac, stopping at a cafe for about 30 minutes, but then continuing towards Bratunac where the convoy stopped. The men were ordered off the bus being shot in batches as they left the bus. The witness was shot but survived, ultimately being able to flee Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the execution site and reach Muslim territory. From the possible additions and clarifications noted for you on a separate sheet of paper, a separate filing, paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, as you entered the place where you were held in Vlasenica, how many people in your estimation remained on the buses?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: About 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later you heard from your wife, I think, that she and your children had been driven to Tisca between Kladanj and Vlasenica from where they'd been allowed to walk to Muslim territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 12. Of the soldiers guarding you as you boarded the buses on the 21st of May, did you see or on those soldiers many types of uniform?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did one of them have a sign saying "Beli Orlovi" and a skill?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. No. It was on the automobile, on the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. That --

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Please. I mean, I didn't really quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to ask you that in any event. The car that accompanied you to the execution site, did that have a marking on the side of it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Not one, several, several signs. Beli Orlovi and also skulls. And it was a white Lada Niva make of car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzafic. You'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzafic, as far as I can see, from 1989 until 1992, you lived in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was temporarily employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 1, in paragraph 4 you say that in March 1992, you heard that the Bosnian Serbs had killed some Muslims at Bascarsija in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was in the first statement. And, well, now I am sure -- I mean, I'm not sure who killed who now, but this killing did take place in Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did some Serbs kill some Muslims in Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, that I don't know, who killed who. I just heard that a killing had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dzafic, but what you heard was the motive that led you to return to your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you planning to return briefly then or did you plan to stay there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I planned to return quite simply to see what was going on and to hear what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what did you hear then? Did you hear a confirmation of this that you stated or did you hear that it was not correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I heard that a killing had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Killing of who?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: A killing happened because there was some kind of a wedding party, and I don't know who killed who.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that it was members of a Serb wedding party that were killed?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's skip some things then, and let's have a look at something else. In paragraph 5, you say that after the Serb forces entered Bratunac, all Muslims were dismissed from their workplaces and that all key positions were taken over by the Serbs, that the former MUP was completely cleansed of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened before that? Did something important happen before that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: In which period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until then. You say that the Serb forces entered Bratunac. So before that.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period before the taking of Bratunac or during the taking of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to be more precise with my question. Do you know what happened to workers of Serb ethnicity and the Serb population in general before the conflict broke out in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know at least that in 1992 all important positions in Bratunac were held by Muslims, as a matter of fact; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's this annex number 2, this list of municipal officials?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Whose officials?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Municipality officials.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Which ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I gave a list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I saw it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I certainly didn't give a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have this information?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, I don't, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the Territorial Defence, that very same year, all command positions from company level up to Chief of Staff were held by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything the fact that the entire military, economic, and political authority was exercised by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the then-authorities in Bratunac adopted specific plans on the blockade of Serb villages and the nearby roads?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all committees of the Party of Democratic Action in local communes already had illegal Crisis Staffs established and attached to them when you came?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Their only duty was to prepare armed activities?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before that the Patriotic League was formed in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that either?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the organisation of military training of Muslims in the territory of the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anything about the accelerated arming of Muslim extremists in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, and I don't believe that any such thing existed, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know who Nezir Muratovic is and Senad Hodzic who was deputy commander of the public security station in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I heard of Senad, but I cannot remember that I know him personally, but I have heard the name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about his activities in terms of obtaining and distributing weapons and carrying out nighttime training in weapons use for Muslim extremists in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Nurif Rizvanovic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
