utterances.text: Do you remember his statement at a particular gathering of locals in Bratunac? And I'm quoting his statement now, that Serb children should be slaughtered if Serbia cannot do anything.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know who the local hodza there is, Munib Efendi Ahmetovic from Vlasenica? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you heard of Osman Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: The name rings a bell. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're not sure. Have you heard of Ramic, the man who was in charge of arming in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I have heard of Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see the programme of the Crisis Staff of the SDA in Bratunac? And among other things, it referred to an elaboration of a blockade of roads and also a list was supposed to be made of Muslim traitors, those who did not want to fight the Serbs, those who were supposed to be liquidated before all of this started and to make a list of those who were capable of combat, also to make lists of weapons.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff of your village, did one exist? Did you know anything about its activities?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know whether this existed at all and whether there was any kind of roster.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you don't know whether it existed, then I'm not going to ask you about it. You say on page 1 of your statement, in line 6 and 7, that the Serbs started taking away the most prominent Muslims from town, and you heard that part of these people were executed and thrown into the Drina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were these people who were taken from town? Can you give me any names?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I think Suljic, but is it a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This man was taken from town?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear this from?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I heard this, but I didn't see it, and I can't remember who I heard it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who took them? Who took this Suco?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I heard it was the members of the army, of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this man was killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you heard over there too?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear about anybody else? Except for this Suco?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I heard about another one who worked as a salesperson. I can't remember now. I knew his name and surname before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you heard that he had also been taken away and killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you can't remember who you heard this from either?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, paragraph 1 of your statement, you say that the village of Glogova was attacked on the 9th of May and that 60 inhabitants of this village were killed, while Krasno Polje was attacked on the 10th of May. That's what you assert?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties in the village of Krasno Polje?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you know anything about fighting in the village of Glogova and the village of Krasno Polje?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were near your village, were they?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I assume that you'd have to know because Glogova is right next to you, also Krasno Polje, and that this was one of the major strongholds of the Muslim extremists.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Muslim extremists? To hear this from you for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there weren't any armed formations there and there wasn't any fighting?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that people who were killed were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that they were Muslim civilians? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the killing of Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. And I don't know that anybody was killed in Krasno Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the municipality of Bratunac? Do you know anything about the killing of Serb civilians there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know, and I don't believe that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody believes that, not even Mrs. Florence Hartmann, because she said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter what Florence Hartmann said. It's not a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it is for the witness that he does not believe that any Serb civilians were killed in the Bratunac municipality. And it is highly relevant, Mr. May, because the opposite side is not accusing Muslim commanders for the killing of civilians because they say that the killing of civilians was never established. So as the witness is now claiming that something like that could not have happened, I have here a document about the Serb victims in Bratunac, and there are a large number of them. I'm not going to read it out. You needn't worry. What did you say? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. At what date are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about 1991 onwards. The Serb victims in Bratunac. But I'm not going to read it all out, so you needn't worry on that score. All I want to do is to read out several names from those lists to try to jog the witness's memory, because he says that none of that ever happened, that Serb civilians were not victims. So, for example -- I'll be very quick about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Radojka Vucetic, born in 1946. She was a housewife. I don't suppose you can question the fact that she was civilian. Then there was Cedo Milutinovic, he was born in 1975 and was a student. Next we have Radojka Jovanovic, a woman, a student, born in 1974. Kosana Zekic, a housewife. Her throat was slit. Otherwise she was born in 1928. So she was an elderly woman. And all this took place in the Bratunac municipality. Stojka Stjepanovic, another housewife, born in 1922. Stanija Vasic, a woman, born in 1930, a housewife. She was born in 1930. Then we have Vujadin Cirkovic, born in 1974, a student. Then we have Dusanka Paunovic, born in 1954, a retiree. The next one is Mileva Dimitric, a housewife. Rada Milosevic, a housewife. She was massacred and lynched. Ilinka Rankovic, also a housewife. Slavka Mladjenovic, housewife. Miloslav Stjepanovic, born in 1919, a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you asking the witness to do?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm asking the witness who said that he does not believe that any Serb civilians were killed in Bratunac, and as I have selected these names from this vast list of killed Serbs whose throats were slit, burnt to death, and so on, mostly women, housewives, children, pensioners, students, and pupils, I'm asking him to tell me whether he knows anything about that. Another one, Kristina Eric, a housewife, burnt to death. A pensioner born in 1920, Risto Popovic. His throat was slit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're not giving evidence yourself. You're cross-examining this witness. The witness can simply be asked if he knows any of these names. It's alleged that these people were killed. Mr. Dzafic, can you help as to that? Do you know anything about any of these allegations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So there's no point reading out any more names. Let's get on with something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I understand that as far as you're concerned there's no point to that, so let me move on. And that's the position taken by the opposite side over there too, that the Muslims are not responsible for the killings of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now do you know who Ejub Ganic is?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Ejub Golic, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Golic.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I've heard of him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he the commander of the infamous Mountain Brigade of the 28th division of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now whether it was infamous or not I don't know, but he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were people from the village of Glogova who made up the Mountain Battalion. Now do you know that they set fire to all the Serb villages and killed hundreds of civilians in Kravica, in Mijesici [phoen], Jelestica, Kijevci, Siljkovici, all those villages Bacici, Bjelovac, Fakovici, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The witness -- the witness -- let the witness answer instead of putting all these allegations to him. Yes, Mr. Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Could you ask questions that relate to my case, what I experienced? As to these other cases, I know nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask about your case. Is it true that in your village the Serbs guaranteed the safety and security of one and all if they is your surrendered their weapons?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, paragraph 5 of your statement, you say that four persons from your village on the 17th of May were taken into custody and taken to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness has not yet asked for a copy of his witness statement but it might be thought prudent -- appropriate for him to have it. And the accused might like to bear in mind for all 92 bis witnesses that paragraphs have been specifically numbered for ease of reference so that if the witness wants to have the statement before him, he can, and the accused should refer to paragraph numbers as well as page numbers because that will enable the witness to go directly to the appropriate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are the B/C/S versions numbered to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so. If they weren't, they should be. I think so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have a copy of the statement. Yes, he's got a copy. Yes, you hear that, Mr. Milosevic, I would echo that. Refer to paragraph numbers. You should have a copies with the numbers beside you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I assume I was very precise and said page 3, paragraph 5 of the statement and the witness confirmed this. He confirmed what he said in his statement, that four persons from his village on the 17th of May, were taken to the police station in Bratunac and held in custody there. I asked him that, and his answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point that's being made is that we now have statements which have numbers against each paragraph. It may be that you are working from an earlier edition which doesn't have the numbers on it. It would therefore be convenient, when you cross-examine witnesses, if you would check to see what the number of the paragraph is. It's much easier to follow a paragraph number than a page and then have to work down. So if you would bear that in mind when you're preparing your cross-examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am bearing this in mind, and it would be much easier for me too if it were so, but I have been given a witness statement without numbered paragraphs from start to finish, and I got the numbered statement and version a moment ago. So I can't now refer and introduce my notes into this latest copy when I have marked the copy I was given first of all. And I have them very precisely noted. So I can't look for them now in this second version of the statement where the paragraphs are numbered from 1 to I don't know how many numbers from start to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you feel you can't assist in that way it will take more time while we all have to find the number, but we will go on in that way. Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you could ask them to supply me with copies that have been marked in the numbers that you insist they should have. It would be much easier for me that way too. But as I say, I just received a copy with the numbering in that way just now -- or, rather, before I started my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as we were saying, four people were taken into custody and to the police station on the 17th of May, Mr. Dzafic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is paragraph 15 in the numbered version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many inhabitants does your village have in total?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: My village numbers 12 houses. As to inhabitants, I can't really say. Twelve households. Now, if you would like me to, I could count through all the members of the households and give you their names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that make about a hundred inhabitants would you say?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did the police look for these four?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, it didn't look for those four alone. It said, "Here you go. Somebody should come to the police station." My father came forward, as did my brother and another cousin. Both cousins. They were neighbours and cousins. They came forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this, Mr. Dzafic. I'm not setting a trap for you through my questions. All I'm saying is I don't know why they asked for four people if they didn't ask for four people specifically. Why did they ask for four inhabitants to step forward?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Do you mean did they ask for by name or did they ask for any four persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said they took four people into custody. Why did they take four people into custody?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: You mean the number or the people concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean why those four. Why were they looking for them at all?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, do you know the reason why these four persons were taken into custody and taken to the police station?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was the reason?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: The reason was because the commander of the sector, Vidoje, he was a policeman, he brought a list with him. And looking at the list, there was the deployment of people in the village. That is to say that those persons were issued weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So they had been issued weapons according to that list from the previous Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. It appeared that they had been issued weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So how many weapons were there in your village, pieces of weapons, how many?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me how many then?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, do you want me to state the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to state the names.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I do, because that makes it easier for me to see how many weapons there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, go ahead. Do what you feel is easiest for you.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: My father had a pistol. He had a permit to carry, a license to carry the weapon. My cousin had a pistol and a rifle. It was a hunting rifle. And he also had a pistol. Once again he had licenses for those weapons. My other cousin also had a hunting rifle and a pistol. And the third cousin did as well. He also had a hunting rifle. He was a neighbour. But he had had the hunting rifle for a long time and so did the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Am I understanding you correctly? Does that mean that, to all intents and purposes, that they were disarmed through the use of force, that they were forcibly disarmed?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Ah no. They handed over their weapons of their own free will following orders, orders from the police station of Bratunac. And the order was that all weapons should be surrendered, and they went of their own free will to the police station to hand over their weapons, and they were given receipts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is that what you mean? Was that when they were taken to the police station? Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. That happened beforehand. When they were taken away and taken off to the police station, they didn't have anything in their possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why did they take them there then?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. They were on this list, and they didn't believe that these people didn't have any weapons on them and they were given an ultimatum of three to five hours to hand in their weapons. If they failed to do so, then the village was not guaranteed safety any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have come to the time to adjourn. Mr. Dzafic, we are going to adjourn now. We must ask you to come back at 9.00 tomorrow morning to finish your evidence. Would you remember --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you remember not to speak to anybody, including the Prosecution, until you've finished your evidence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know there will be timetable problems with the next witness arising from the fact that we've overrun with the last couple of witnesses. There are two witnesses currently scheduled for tomorrow. I can't say at the moment whether there will be any application to change the present order so that it's the reverse way round. It might be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would regard that with some seriousness. Some consideration must be given to others involved in this trial. Now, that witness has been prepared for a long time. I don't see why he shouldn't be here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His trouble is his return date and I just -- I've received a message. I don't know what the consequence of it is, and I don't know if there is any chance of any more court time available for tomorrow, but I'm just alerting the Chamber to the fact that there's a problem looming about the amount of time. I'll go and deal with it as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would, because I don't understand what problem there can be knowing the circumstances of the witness. He should be made available. Maybe you will get some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're thinking of another witness. Yes. The witness Your Honour had in mind is unavoidably available as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's the witness after that. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I know the order of witnesses after this witness if it's being changed in relation to the list I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. received earlier on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is precisely that that we have expressed concern about and indicated our views. We will hear more tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But order is as is at present but if we have to make any application to change, we'll let everybody know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It should be stabilised. Very well. Tomorrow morning at 9.00, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
